If cross-regional collaboration is meant to share best practices, why are we still copying tech and dashboards instead of transferring living wages, local budgets, and offline fallbacks?  
What would it take for joint funding formulas to penalize single-point failures—like one lab tech or van—and reward communities that pivot when chaos hits?  
How do we ensure that “shared models” don’t just export Vermont’s fragility under new branding but actually replicate Arizona’s elder-led decision-making power?  
Can we measure collaboration success by whether a region survives a snowstorm or staff walkout—not just whether their spreadsheets align?  
Why aren’t we tying regional grants to burnout rates, childcare access, and whether ride vouchers work without cell service?  
And if true resilience means systems absorb failure before it reaches patients, shouldn’t collaboration start by handing over real control—not just protocols—to the people who live through the breakdowns?
conversation.subtopic: Cross-regional collaboration models to share best practices in rapid case identification and contact management.

conversation.content: Let’s shift to how funding formulas themselves sabotage cross-regional collaboration—because if joint grants still reward speed over sustainability, we’re just incentivizing regions to copy shiny tech while ignoring the human infrastructure that actually keeps systems alive. Arizona’s elders didn’t succeed because they had better dashboards—they succeeded because they controlled budgets, adapted in real time, and weren’t punished when the internet died. Yet most collaborative funding still ties payouts to lab turnaround times or mobile unit deployment, not staff retention, offline voucher functionality, or whether childcare slots are pre-booked. That’s not collaboration—it’s coercion disguised as best practice.

conversation.content: Actually, the whole “seasonal patterns” angle is being overused as a distraction—yes, flu spikes in winter or RSV surges in fall matter, but they’re not the root cause of system collapse. The real issue is that we keep designing for predictable seasons while ignoring the unpredictable human breakdowns: a lab tech quitting in July, a van breaking down in April, or elders burning out after 18 months of no raises. If Vermont’s system failed during a snowstorm, it wasn’t because winter came—it was because the funding model treated staff and logistics as disposable until chaos hit. Arizona’s tribal model didn’t succeed by forecasting infection rates; it succeeded by embedding decision-making where care happens, regardless of season. Until we stop blaming weather and start tying funding to staff retention, offline backups, and local power, we’re just rearranging seasonal charts while the infrastructure rots from within. Speed metrics won’t save us when the dispatcher quits—and no amount of “proactive planning” fixes that if the plan doesn’t include living wages. Equity isn’t about anticipating flu season—it’s about building systems that don’t collapse when people leave, phones die, or vans stall. Let’s stop pretending seasonal data is the answer when the real vulnerability is human, not meteorological.

SILVER SPRING, Md. - Rear Adm.  (Ret.) Tim Ziemer, the U.S. Global  Malaria Coordinator, President‟s  Malaria Initiative, visited the Naval  Medical Research Center ( NMRC ),  November 29, for a brief on the  current malaria vaccine research  efforts and to tour the facility. He was  interested in learning more about the  malaria program at the laboratory.  Capt. John Sanders, NMRC  commanding officer, provided a  general overview of the NMRC  enterprise with emphasis on the  infectious diseases research efforts,  specifically in the area of malaria.  “The NMRC malaria research  program is at the forefront of malaria

One notable collaboration is being spearheaded by  Cmdr. Jonathan Forsberg (NMRC, Operational and Un- dersea Medicine Directorate), who is working with a com- pany to explore a novel mode of anchoring prosthetics.  This project could produce important results for amputees.  Another collaboration being led by Lt. Roxanne Burrus  ( U.S. Naval Medical Research Unit No. 6 , Lima, Peru)  involves Duke University and focuses on evaluating the  effects of changing demography and land use on malaria  transmission. This is an important issue in light of the  prevalence of malaria in developing countries and is  important to the health of deployed war fighters. An addi- tional malaria-focused collaboration is being headed by Lt.  R. Vince Gerbasi (NMRC, Infectious Diseases Director- ate), who is using mass spectrometry to identify novel  antigens to be used as potential vaccine candidates.  Lastly, Dr Bjorn Song ( Naval Medical Research Unit-San  Antonio ) is leading a collaboration focused on exploring  the use of a synthetic oxygen-carrying fluid to reduce  tissue damage occurring in response to hemorrhagic  shock.

Since 2010, Navy biomedical researchers have been  collaborating with the Liberian Institute of Biomedical Re- search (LIBR) on two research projects funded by the  Armed Forces Health Surveillance Center/Global Emerging  Infections System (AFHSC-GEIS). content.text: CAIRO - U.S. Naval Medical Research Unit No. 3   ( NAMRU-3 ) is playing an important role in medical research  capacity building in Liberia, which is recovering from a brutal  14-year civil war that devastated the country‟s infrastructure.

SAN DIEGO - The Expeditionary Medicine Modeling,  Simulation, and Analysis group at the Naval Health Re- search Center ( NHRC ) completed development of the Pa- tient Condition Occurrence Frequency (PCOF) tool. In Oc- tober, the tool was presented to the Force Health Protec- tion and Readiness, Strategic Analysis Working Group Of- fice of the Assistant Secretary of Defense, Health Affairs as  part of the verification, validation, and accreditation (VV&A)  plan for service acceptance. The working group forwarded  their recommendation for accreditation to the Force Health  Protection Integration Council. Once accredited, NHRC‟s  PCOF tool will be approved as the Joint patient occurrence  generating application.

Recently NSMRL acquired NAVSEA‟s new DP1/2 diving system. The DP1/2 is a surface supplied air system that  includes communications capability with the diver. This provides enhanced capabilities for underwater investigations,  since the diver can receive directions and report back in real time to the topside personnel orchestrating the experi- mentation. In return, NSMRL is testing the equipment for general Navy diving use and validating/revising operating in- structions for clarity, proper sequencing and procedural accuracy. NSMRL has a history of research in underwater  communications, and with the acquisition of this diving system, we harnessed another improved means of communica- tions with our divers.
